questions.stem: The main roles of households in the economy are to:
options: supply factors of production and buy goods and services
produce goods and services and pay wages to workers
collect taxes and provide essential public services
lend savings to banks and set the level of interest rates
questions.explanation: Households own and supply land, labour, capital and enterprise, and use the income to buy goods and services. Producing output and paying wages is the role of businesses.

questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that:
options: consumers always buy the good that gives the greatest total utility
each additional unit consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before
each additional unit consumed adds more satisfaction than the one before
total satisfaction falls as soon as a person consumes a second unit
questions.explanation: The fourth slice of pizza adds less extra satisfaction than the first. Total utility can still rise while marginal utility falls, as long as marginal utility is positive.

questions.stem: A student's total utility from slices of pizza is 20, 35, 45 and 50 for one to four slices. The marginal utility of the third slice is:
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility: 45 - 35 = 10. Total utility after three slices is 45, and 15 is the marginal utility of the second slice.

questions.stem: A consumer is choosing between more coffee and more muffins. Making a choice at the margin means the consumer compares:
options: the total satisfaction from all coffees with that from all muffins
the total amount spent on coffee this year with the amount on muffins
the average price of coffee in the market with the price of muffins
the extra satisfaction per dollar of another coffee and another muffin
questions.explanation: A utility-maximising consumer spends each extra dollar where it adds the most satisfaction, so decisions depend on marginal utility relative to price, not on totals or averages.

questions.stem: A shopper pays more for coffee certified as fairly traded, even though cheaper coffee tastes the same. This shows consumers acting as:
options: purely self-interested utility maximisers
producers maximising profit
free riders on a public good
socially and ethically motivated agents
questions.explanation: Consumers' choices are also shaped by values, culture and social norms, not only by their own material satisfaction. This challenges the assumption that consumers are purely self-interested.

questions.stem: When income rises, demand for a normal good:
options: decreases
stays the same
becomes zero
increases
questions.explanation: Most goods are normal goods, so people buy more as incomes rise. Demand for inferior goods falls as incomes rise because people switch to preferred alternatives.

questions.stem: As their incomes rise, many households buy less home-brand bread and more premium bread. Home-brand bread is:
options: a Veblen good
a public good
an inferior good
a normal good
questions.explanation: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because consumers trade up to higher-quality substitutes. Premium bread here behaves as a normal good.

questions.stem: Demand for a luxury handbag rises after the maker raises its price, because buyers value it as a sign of status. The handbag is:
options: a Veblen good
an inferior good
a merit good
a common-pool resource
questions.explanation: A Veblen good is valued partly because it is expensive, so a higher price can increase demand, an exception to the law of demand. Demand for inferior goods falls as income rises, not as price rises.

questions.stem: Saving is best described as:
options: money paid to the government in the form of income tax each year
spending on capital goods by businesses to expand production
deferred consumption: income not spent now so it can be spent later
spending more than current income by borrowing or using past savings
questions.explanation: Households save to consume in the future, such as in retirement. Spending more than current income is dissaving, and business spending on capital goods is investment.

questions.stem: A retired couple spends $60,000 a year while receiving $40,000 in income, drawing on their superannuation. This is:
options: dissaving
saving
investment
a transfer payment
questions.explanation: When consumption exceeds income, households run down past savings or borrow, which is dissaving. Retirees commonly dissave as they draw down their super.

questions.stem: During a recession every household decides to save more to protect itself. The paradox of thrift suggests that:
options: total spending falls, incomes fall and total saving may not rise at all
total spending rises, incomes rise and total saving rises even more
interest rates must rise, attracting more saving into the banking system
each household is worse off, but the economy as a whole is better off
questions.explanation: One household saving more is prudent, but if all do so, spending and therefore incomes fall, so total saving may be unchanged or lower. What is rational for one can harm the whole economy.

questions.stem: Consumer sovereignty means that:
options: the government decides which goods households are allowed to purchase
consumers are protected by law from buying goods that may harm them
consumers' spending decisions determine what goods and services are produced
producers decide what goods will be made and then persuade consumers to buy them
questions.explanation: In a market economy, firms that produce what consumers want earn profits, so consumer choices steer resources. Consumer protection laws are a separate role of government.

questions.stem: A subscription service makes signing up a single click but cancelling requires a phone call during business hours. This design is an example of:
options: a nudge that strengthens consumer sovereignty
a merit good that is underprovided by markets
an economy of scale that lowers the firm's costs
a sludge that challenges consumer sovereignty
questions.explanation: A sludge adds friction that steers people towards choices that benefit the firm rather than themselves. It weakens consumer sovereignty because outcomes reflect the design, not consumers' true preferences.

questions.stem: How can heavy marketing challenge consumer sovereignty?
options: It gives consumers complete information, so they always choose the best product
It lowers the prices of all goods, so consumers can buy more of everything
It removes product differentiation, so consumers see all brands as identical
It shapes consumers' wants, so firms influence demand rather than respond to it
questions.explanation: Advertising can create wants and brand loyalty, so producers partly decide what consumers buy. This weakens the idea that consumer preferences independently direct production.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the link between consumption, income and wellbeing?
options: Higher income always lowers wellbeing because it brings longer working hours
Higher income and consumption raise wellbeing, but by less as income keeps rising
Each extra dollar of income raises wellbeing by the same amount at every level
Wellbeing depends only on consumption, so leisure and relationships do not matter
questions.explanation: Extra income matters most to those on low incomes, consistent with diminishing marginal utility; health, leisure, security and relationships also shape wellbeing. That is why measures beyond GDP are used.

questions.stem: Which factor is most likely to increase the supply of labour from households?
options: Lower levels of education and training
Higher wages and better non-wage benefits
Less affordable and less available childcare
Less flexible working hours in most jobs
questions.explanation: Better pay and conditions encourage more people to work and to work more hours. Poor access to childcare and inflexible workplaces discourage participation.

questions.stem: Many parents with young children would like to work more hours but cannot find affordable childcare. This is a:
options: disincentive to workforce participation
rise in occupational mobility
fall in the demand for labour
non-wage benefit of employment
questions.explanation: When the cost or availability of care makes work unviable, labour supply falls, especially among women. Childcare subsidies aim to reduce this barrier.

questions.stem: A worker cannot move to a mining job in another state because housing there is too expensive. This illustrates low:
options: geographic mobility of labour
occupational mobility of labour
marginal utility of labour
productivity of capital
questions.explanation: Geographic mobility is the ability to move between places for work. Occupational mobility is the ability to move between types of jobs, which depends on skills and training.

questions.stem: A factory worker retrains as an electrician through a TAFE course. This most directly improves the worker's:
options: occupational mobility
geographic mobility
non-wage benefits
consumer sovereignty
questions.explanation: Gaining new skills lets workers move between occupations as the structure of the economy changes. Moving between places is geographic mobility.

questions.stem: The main role of businesses in the economy is to:
options: combine factors of production to produce goods and services
supply labour to households in return for wages and salaries
redistribute income through taxes and transfer payments
determine the cash rate and the supply of money
questions.explanation: Businesses organise land, labour, capital and enterprise to produce output, paying factor incomes in return. Redistribution is a government role and the cash rate is set by the RBA.

questions.stem: A cafe owner's revenue is $300,000 and explicit costs are $220,000. She gave up a $90,000 salary to run the cafe. Her accounting profit and economic profit are:
questions.explanation: Accounting profit = 300,000 - 220,000 = $80,000. Economic profit also deducts the opportunity cost of her forgone salary: 80,000 - 90,000 = -$10,000, so she could earn more elsewhere.

questions.stem: The key difference between economic profit and accounting profit is that economic profit:
options: also adds the value of government subsidies the business has received
is calculated before any explicit costs such as wages are deducted
is calculated only for public enterprises owned by the government
also deducts implicit costs, such as the owner's forgone salary
questions.explanation: Accounting profit subtracts only explicit, paid costs. Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs too, showing whether resources are earning as much as their next best use.

questions.stem: A business owned and run by the government, such as a state-owned water utility, is:
options: a private enterprise
a sole trader
a cooperative
a public enterprise
questions.explanation: Public enterprises are owned by governments, while private enterprises are owned by individuals or shareholders. Businesses producing similar goods are grouped into industries.

questions.stem: A business's productivity is a measure of:
options: the profit earned by a business per dollar of sales
output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked
the total quantity of goods produced in the economy
the total number of hours worked by all employees
questions.explanation: Productivity measures efficiency: producing more from the same inputs. Total output can rise simply by using more inputs, with no gain in productivity.

questions.stem: Why is productivity growth important for living standards?
options: It raises prices, which increases the profits and wages of all businesses
It reduces output, which lowers the use of natural resources and pollution
It increases the hours people must work to produce the same goods
It lets real incomes rise, as more is produced in each hour worked
questions.explanation: When each worker produces more, firms can pay higher wages and stay profitable, and real incomes rise. Productivity growth is the main source of long-run gains in living standards.

questions.stem: A warehouse gives each worker an automated picking robot, so the amount of capital per worker rises. This is:
options: a diseconomy of scale
a fall in factor mobility
a non-wage benefit
capital deepening
questions.explanation: Capital deepening means increasing capital per worker, which tends to raise labour productivity. Diseconomies of scale are rises in average cost as a firm grows too large.

questions.stem: A large supermarket chain can buy stock in bulk at lower prices per unit than a small grocer. This is:
options: an internal economy of scale
an external economy of scale
an internal diseconomy of scale
capital deepening
questions.explanation: Internal economies arise within the firm as it grows, such as bulk buying, specialisation and cheaper finance. External economies arise from the growth of the whole industry or area.

questions.stem: Many software firms locate in one area, attracting a pool of skilled workers and specialist suppliers that lowers costs for every firm there. This is:
options: an external economy of scale
an internal economy of scale
an external diseconomy of scale
a fall in productivity
questions.explanation: External economies benefit all firms in an industry or region as it expands, regardless of each firm's size. If congestion and rising rents later raised costs, that would be an external diseconomy.

questions.stem: A company grows so large that communication becomes slow, decisions take longer and staff motivation falls, raising average costs. This is:
options: an internal diseconomy of scale
an external economy of scale
capital deepening
the technical optimum
questions.explanation: Beyond a certain size, coordination and management problems within the firm push average costs up. These are internal diseconomies, shown by the rising part of the LRAC curve.

questions.stem: On a long-run average cost (LRAC) curve, the technical optimum is:
options: the output at which diseconomies of scale first appear
the output at which long-run average cost is at its lowest
the output at which total cost is at its highest
the output at which the firm earns zero accounting profit
questions.explanation: The technical optimum is the lowest point of the U-shaped LRAC curve. To its left, economies of scale lower average cost; to its right, diseconomies raise it.

questions.stem: A firm's LRAC curve slopes downward as output rises from 1,000 to 5,000 units, then upward beyond 5,000. A firm producing 2,000 units could lower its average cost by:
options: expanding output well beyond 8,000 units
keeping output fixed at 2,000 units
expanding output towards 5,000 units
reducing output below 2,000 units
questions.explanation: Between 1,000 and 5,000 units the firm is gaining economies of scale, so growth lowers average cost until the technical optimum at 5,000. Beyond that, diseconomies raise average cost.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a non-wage benefit of employment?
options: Flexible working hours and paid parental leave
An hourly wage well above the award rate
A weekly salary paid into a bank account
Overtime paid at time and a half
questions.explanation: Non-wage benefits are rewards other than pay, such as flexibility, leave, training, a car or a pleasant workplace. Hourly wages, salaries and overtime are wage benefits.

questions.stem: Which is an argument for a more equitable distribution of income from work, such as a minimum wage?
options: It removes the need for any government spending on welfare payments
It protects low-paid workers and supports their living standards
It encourages employers to hire more low-skilled workers at higher cost
It makes wage outcomes reflect each worker's productivity more closely
questions.explanation: A minimum wage provides a floor that protects workers with little bargaining power. Critics argue that setting it too high may reduce hiring of low-skilled workers.

questions.stem: The demand for labour is called a derived demand because:
options: it is set by the government through the national minimum wage decision
it is derived from the number of people of working age in the economy
it depends only on the wage that workers are willing to accept
it depends on the demand for the goods and services that labour produces
questions.explanation: Firms hire workers to produce output, so when demand for output rises, so does demand for labour. Population affects the supply of labour, not the demand.

questions.stem: A rise in wages relative to the cost of machinery is most likely to cause businesses to:
options: stop investing in all new machinery and equipment
increase hiring because higher wages raise productivity
substitute capital for labour, reducing demand for workers
substitute labour for capital, increasing demand for workers
questions.explanation: When labour becomes relatively more expensive, firms have an incentive to automate. The relative cost of labour and capital is a key factor affecting the demand for labour.

questions.stem: The spread of artificial intelligence tools is most likely to affect the demand for labour by:
options: having no effect, because AI cannot perform any tasks done by workers
reducing demand for some routine tasks while increasing demand for new skills
increasing demand for all types of labour equally across every industry
reducing demand for all types of labour equally across every industry
questions.explanation: AI and automation can replace workers in routine or predictable tasks but complement workers in others and create new roles. The effect differs across occupations, which can cause structural change.

questions.stem: Which government policy is most likely to increase the demand for labour by businesses?
options: A tax concession that lowers the cost of buying labour-saving machinery
A rise in the national minimum wage well above productivity growth
A wage subsidy paid to firms that hire long-term unemployed people
A large rise in the payroll tax that firms pay on their wage bills
questions.explanation: A wage subsidy lowers the cost of employing workers, encouraging firms to hire. Payroll tax and cheaper labour-saving machinery tend to reduce the demand for labour.
